fixes.explanation: That's his answer. When Saul asks who he is, he says, “I am an Amalekite.” Verse 1 says David had just come back from the slaughter of the Amalekites.

That's it. The man says, “…I took the crown that was on his head and the band that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord.” He says he brought them to David. That's what he says he took from Saul.

That's true. David takes hold of his own clothes and tears them, and “…all the men who were with him did the same.” His men tore their clothes right along with him. Verse 12 says they mourned and wept and fasted until evening.

Actually it's true, friend. David tears his own clothes, and the text says “…all the men who were with him did the same.” So the men with him tore their clothes right along with him. The text puts every one of them in it.

That's right. The text says they mourned “…for Saul and his son Jonathan, and for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.” So it wasn't only those two. They wept and fasted until evening for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel too.

No question about leaving the battle shows up here. David asks, “Why were you not afraid to lift your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?” That's a pointed question, and it goes straight at what the man said he did.

That's right. David “…ordered that the sons of Judah be taught the Song of the Bow.” That's the name of the lament, and it's written in the Book of Jashar. Verse 17 says David took up this lament for Saul and his son Jonathan. He wanted it learned, not just sung once and forgotten.

Yes. David sings, “Tell it not in Gath; proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, and the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.” Gath and Ashkelon are the places he names. He asks that it not be told there, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice.

The song doesn't say that. David's reason is, “…lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, and the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.” Gath and Ashkelon are the places he names. He asks that it not be told there, lest they rejoice.

That's a thoughtful guess, but the song gives a different reason. It says, “…lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, and the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.” Gath and Ashkelon are the places he names. David's concern is the daughters of the Philistines rejoicing.

Not in this song. David sings, “Saul and Jonathan, beloved and delightful in life, were not divided in death.” And look at what he's doing. He takes up a lament for them and orders it taught, which is not what you do with someone you want forgotten.
